summary: Proposes a SIP event package that lets a SIP endpoint subscribe to be notified when a particular HTTP resource is created, changed, or deleted. This lets applications that combine SIP and HTTP servers learn about changes in near real time instead of repeatedly polling.

eli5.summary: Instead of checking a mailbox every few minutes, you ask to be told the moment something new arrives. This lets phone-style SIP programs get told when a web page or file changes.

questions: how to subscribe to http resource changes using sip
what is the sip http-monitor event package
how to get notified when an http resource changes

subtitle: How a SIP client asks to be told when a web resource is created, changed or deleted, instead of polling it.

tldr.problem: Systems that mix SIP and HTTP servers often need to learn, in near real time, when a specific HTTP resource is created, changed or deleted, and polling is a poor way to do that.
tldr.mechanism: The HTTP server hands out a SIP or SIPS URI in a Link header (relation types monitor and monitor-group). The client sends a SUBSCRIBE for the http-monitor event package to that URI and receives NOTIFY messages carrying a message/http body that describes the resource.
tldr.outcome: Clients get change notifications over SIP while HTTP is still used to fetch the content itself, unless the subscription asks for bodies with body=true.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: SHOULD NOT exceed once per second

today: RFC 5989 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Watch an HTTP Resource Over SIP
sections.content:
RFC 5989 targets systems where the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is tightly coupled with HTTP servers. A typical case: user agent terminals store service-related data in an HTTP tree, and need to be told when that data changes so they can adjust their local behavior and user interface.

The RFC builds on the SIP Event Framework (RFC 3265). Subscriptions do not necessarily carry the resource content. When they do not, HTTP is still the protocol that transfers the content. The RFC also defines how the right SIP or SIPS URI for a subscription is discovered from the HTTP server.
sections.eli5: A web page can change at any time. This RFC gives phone-style programs a way to say 'tell me when it changes', so they do not have to keep peeking.

sections.title: Finding the SIP URI From an HTTP URL
sections.content:
The hard part is knowing which SIP URI matches a given HTTP URL. The RFC makes the HTTP server responsible: it picks the SIP URI and returns it in an HTTP transaction, using link relations. The RFC defines two new relation types, monitor and monitor-group. They can be carried in the HTTP Link header field, the HTML <link/> element or the Atom <atom:link/> element. Clients using this mechanism MUST support the Link header field. Clients that process HTML SHOULD support the HTML element, and those that process Atom SHOULD support the Atom element.

For a single resource, the server returns a monitor link holding a SIP or SIPS URI in a successful response to a GET or HEAD. The client uses that URI in a SUBSCRIBE. A response may contain several monitoring link relations for different protocols, so implementors are told to process all of them and pick the one that matches their preferred change-monitoring protocol.

For several resources, a server can return a monitor-group URI, which corresponds to a Resource List Server (RLS) that MUST support request-contained resource lists as in RFC 5367. A server that returns monitor-group MUST also return a monitor link. The client groups resources by their monitor-group URI and sends one subscription per group, with a URI list of the individual monitor URIs. Clients may alternatively use the mechanisms of RFC 4662 and RFC 5367 with no special server support, though that is often less efficient.
sections.eli5: When you ask the web server for a page, it also tells you a special phone number for change alerts. For lots of pages on one server, it gives one shared number so you only call once.

sections.title: The http-monitor Event Package
sections.content:
The event package is named http-monitor. It defines one parameter on the Event header field, body, whose value is true or false. When it is true in a SUBSCRIBE, the client asks for a message-body inside the message/http bodies of NOTIFY messages. A server MAY include one, or decline based on local policy, for example to avoid bodies above a small size. When the parameter is absent it is taken as false. It concerns the HTTP message-body, not the SIP message body. SUBSCRIBE requests carry no body.

Subscription duration is left to the subscriber. For fast-changing resources the RFC suggests durations on the order of 1800 to 3600 seconds, so a failed subscription is recovered quickly. For slow-changing ones, expirations as long as 604800 seconds (one week) or longer may make sense. If a subscription has no expires value, the notifier applies local policy, and 86400 seconds (one day) would not be unreasonable.

Other rules: authorization on SUBSCRIBE should typically match the HTTP server's own access policy for the resource. Notifiers SHOULD NOT send notifications more frequently than once every second. If a SUBSCRIBE is forked, which is called aberrant here because multiple notifiers for one HTTP resource make no sense, the subscriber SHOULD terminate all but one subscription.
sections.eli5: You choose how long your alert signup lasts: short if the page changes a lot, long if it hardly changes. The alerts also never come faster than once a second.

sections.title: What a NOTIFY Contains
sections.content:
By default a NOTIFY body has content type message/http, and it reflects a subset of the response an HTTP HEAD on the resource would return. It SHOULD contain at least one of ETag or Content-MD5, and a Last-Modified field is RECOMMENDED. It MUST contain a Content-Location field identifying the monitored resource. It MUST NOT include an HTTP message-body unless the subscription asked for one with body=true.

The start line tells what happened. A rename uses the 3xx response a HEAD would give (for example 301 Moved Permanently), and the notification SHOULD carry a Location field with the new name. A deletion uses the 4xx response a HEAD would give (for example 404 Not Found or 410 Gone). If the notifier has too little information to say anything useful, it MUST send a zero-byte body.

The subscriber uses the message to update its view of the resource. Usually that means invalidating its cached copy. Whether to fetch a new copy is up to the subscriber.
sections.eli5: The alert is a short note: what the page is called, a fingerprint of its newest version, and when it last changed. If the page moved or was thrown away, the note says that instead.

sections.title: An Example Message Flow
sections.content:
The RFC includes a flow, for illustration only, that is not part of the specification. A client sends an HTTP GET for http://www.example.com/pet-profiles/alpacas/. The response carries a Link header with rel="monitor". The client sends a SUBSCRIBE with Event: http-monitor to that SIP URI, gets a 200 OK, then an initial NOTIFY with the current state. The client can compare ETag, Content-MD5 or Last-Modified with what it got over HTTP to confirm it has the latest version.

Later the document changes. The web server tells the SIP Events server with a SIP PUBLISH, though the RFC notes that any other means of conveying this would be equally valid. The SIP Events server then sends a NOTIFY to the client, which may fetch a fresh copy or simply mark its old copy as out of date.
sections.eli5: You ask for a page and get a phone number for alerts. You sign up. When someone edits the page, the web server whispers to the alert desk, and the desk calls you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An unsecured Link header field is not secure, private or integrity-protected, so servers are cautioned not to treat its value as a token proving a subscriber is authorized. It can also be tampered with or forged in transit, so clients should think about forged notifications, which is especially a worry when notifications include entity state (body=true).

Because state of an HTTP resource can now be learned over another protocol and possibly another server, access control MUST carry over: if the HTTP resource is restricted, the SIP route to its state MUST be restricted the same way. Likewise if the resource is protected in transit by HTTP over TLS, the SIP subscription MUST have appropriate encryption or integrity protection. The RFC names the SIPS URI scheme and S/MIME bodies as examples.
sections.eli5: If a secret page needs a password, the alert service must ask for one too. Otherwise a stranger could learn about the page through the side door.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers two Link Relation Types, monitor (a resource that can be used to monitor changes in an HTTP resource) and monitor-group (a resource for monitoring changes in a specified group of HTTP resources), using the registry created by Web Linking (RFC 5988).

It also adds the SIP event package http-monitor to the SIP Events registry, and the Event header field parameter body to the SIP Header Field Parameters and Parameter Values registry.
sections.eli5: New names get written in the official lists so that nobody else uses them for something different.
